title: Deterministic fully dynamic connectivity with polylogarithmic worst-case updates
formal:
Does there exist a finite deterministic word-RAM program \(A\), with fixed positive integer constants \(C,c,d,a\), such that for every integer \(n\ge2\) it maintains an initially empty simple undirected graph on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) under every finite valid online sequence of edge insertions, edge deletions and pairwise connectivity queries, with all the following guarantees?
\[\begin{aligned}
 \text{initialization time}&\le Cn^d,\\
 \text{total stored words at every time}&\le Cn^d,\\
 \text{time of each individual operation}&\le C(\log_2 n)^c.
\end{aligned}\]
Every query must return the exact connectivity bit. Initialization receives only \(n\); the word size is \(w=\lceil a\log_2 n\rceil\), and computation uses the machine conventions below. All constants and the same finite program are chosen before \(n\) or the operation sequence. Give a complete Lean proof of this existence proposition or its logical negation.
definitions:
A graph state is a set \(E\subseteq\{\{u,v\}:u,v\in[n],\ u\ne v\}\), initially empty. An operation has a tag and two vertex labels, each supplied as one word. A valid \(\operatorname{insert}(u,v)\) requires distinct endpoints and an absent edge, and adds that edge. A valid \(\operatorname{delete}(u,v)\) requires a present edge and removes it. A query \(\operatorname{connected}(u,v)\) is valid for any \(u,v\in[n]\) and outputs one bit. Its answer is one exactly when there is a finite sequence \(u=x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_k=v\), with \(k\ge0\), whose consecutive pairs are edges of the current graph. In particular, a vertex is connected to itself. The graph has no additional promise on density, planarity, degree or expansion.

The machine must finish the current operation before the next is supplied. No operation count, future sequence, or complete input graph is available during initialization. The guarantee applies to every finite valid sequence of arbitrary length, including sequences selected using all previously observable states and answers. Persistent memory is bounded in terms of \(n\) alone, independently of the elapsed number of operations. Past output is write-only and cannot serve as free external storage.

Fix a word RAM with a finite instruction list and a fixed finite number of word registers. Words are unsigned integers in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\); memory addresses are also words. Each indirect load or store, register copy, comparison, conditional branch, Boolean bitwise operation, shift, and arithmetic operation on at most two words costs one step. Arithmetic primitives are addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer quotient and remainder. Addition, subtraction and multiplication return their result modulo \(2^w\); quotient and remainder use unsigned integer division and a zero divisor causes failure. A left shift discards bits outside the word; a right shift fills with zeros; either returns zero when the shift amount is at least \(w\). Reading an input word and writing the query bit also cost one step. The finite program can contain fixed integer constants, interpreted modulo \(2^w\), but has no oracle, random instruction, advice string or input-size-dependent instruction table. Any longer arithmetic computation pays for all constituent instructions.

Mutable registers and allocated memory, including every table and representation of the graph, count toward the stated space bound. Initially they contain only zeros except for the input \(n\); data-dependent initialization, allocation and zeroing of allocated words are charged. Every addressed location must be allocated and have a representable address. The fixed coefficient \(a\) may be chosen sufficiently large for the program's polynomial space; it cannot depend on \(n\) or sequence length. Polynomial preprocessing may depend only on \(n\), and all its computation and stored output count toward the initialization and space bounds. The program and its fixed finite control are independent of \(n\).

Time includes all graph maintenance, rebuilding, memory management, query computation and response output performed during that operation. No background work between operations is free. The operation bound is a worst-case bound for each individual call, not an average over a sequence or an expectation. Using positive integer constants is a normalization of the original polynomial-space and polylogarithmic-time bounds: enlarging constants or exponents absorbs fixed factors and small input sizes. It imposes no graph restriction.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of either
\[\exists A\ \exists C,c,d,a\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge2\ \forall s\in\mathcal S_n,\quad \operatorname{Guarantees}(A,C,c,d,a,n,s),\]
or its logical negation. Here \(A\) ranges over the finite deterministic programs just defined, \(\mathcal S_n\) is the set of all finite valid operation sequences, and \(\operatorname{Guarantees}\) includes initialization, termination, exact answers, memory use and the per-operation bounds in the statement. A positive answer must establish all guarantees for one program and constants that work for every \(n,s\). A negative answer must rule out every such program and every constant choice, equivalently show that each candidate fails a required guarantee for some size and finite valid sequence, with the empty sequence also testing initialization. Failure to terminate is a failure of the applicable time bound.

All memory and running-time statements must refer to the specified machine semantics. A lower bound for a restricted family of implementations, a single counterexample to one proposed algorithm, or a theorem requiring an unproved complexity assumption does not negate the full proposition. An amortized, randomized, expected-time, restricted-graph or offline guarantee does not prove it. This is an existence question, with no numerical tolerance or weaker intermediate target.
why: Exact dynamic connectivity is a basic test of whether a graph data structure can guarantee uniformly low latency without randomness. The question separates efficient processing of a long sequence from a fast response after every individual change, and is relevant to graph algorithms that call connectivity as a subroutine.

importance.reason: A foundational dynamic-graph frontier directly relevant to data structures, with a new randomized breakthrough and an explicit remaining deterministic bottleneck.

progress.text: Holm–de Lichtenberg–Thorup obtain deterministic \(O(\log^2 n)\) amortized updates for fully dynamic connectivity.
Pătraşcu–Demaine give logarithmic cell-probe lower bounds and update–query tradeoffs, even for disjoint paths.
Kapron–King–Mountjoy obtain polylogarithmic worst-case operation bounds with randomization and one-sided query error.
The deterministic balanced-cut preprint establishes \(n^{o(1)}\) worst-case dynamic connectivity in Theorem 1.5; the work appears at FOCS 2020.
The expected-time connectivity preprint gives its Las Vegas theorem and a conditional deterministic theorem. The inspected arXiv record remains version 1.
FOCS 2026 lists a new polylogarithmic worst-case connectivity paper. Its determinism, error and model guarantees were not obtainable from the inspected announcement.

status_note: Uncertain after review on 15 September 2026. The inspected October 2025 preprint, published at SODA 2026, explicitly leaves the deterministic polylogarithmic worst-case target open and proves an expected randomized bound plus a conditional deterministic theorem. However, the official FOCS 2026 accepted list and an author page now announce a closely matching new paper by Meierhans, Probst Gutenberg and Yeh. The inspected listings contain no theorem statement or manuscript link; bounded searches did not obtain its full text. Its determinism, error guarantee and exact model therefore remain unchecked. The card stays active with a complete formulation, without treating an announcement title as a matching solution or asserting current openness from the older source.

context_blocks.text: Connectivity asks whether two vertices lie in the same component, not for a shortest path or an explicit list of all vertices in that component. Deleting an edge can change this answer for many pairs simultaneously. The required output is still only the queried bit; the target concerns how much work must be charged to each operation.

Holm, de Lichtenberg and Thorup give a deterministic structure with \(O(\log^2 n)\) amortized update time and \(O(\log n/\log\log n)\) connectivity query time. Their guarantee controls the total work over a sequence, while permitting an expensive individual update. It does not establish the per-operation guarantee asked here.

Kapron, King and Mountjoy give worst-case bounds \(O(\log^4 n)\) for insertion, \(O(\log^5 n)\) for deletion and \(O(\log n/\log\log n)\) for queries. Their randomized structure has one-sided error: a reported connection is valid, but a reported disconnection can be wrong with small probability. This does not give the exact deterministic guarantee.

Chuzhoy and coauthors establish deterministic \(n^{o(1)}\) worst-case update time. This notation permits functions growing more quickly than every fixed power of \(\log n\), for example \(\exp(\sqrt{\log n})\). Consequently a subpolynomial bound alone leaves a gap to the fixed polylogarithm in this card.

Meierhans and Probst Gutenberg’s SODA 2026 Theorem 1.1 is Las Vegas: it maintains a correct spanning forest with polylogarithmic expected worst-case update time. Its guarantee even allows an adaptive adversary observing the internal state and random bits. The expectation is over the algorithm’s randomness for an operation, rather than amortization over operations; it remains different from a deterministic bound on every execution. Theorem 1.3 gives a conditional deterministic result, not an unconditional resolution of this card.

Pătraşcu and Demaine prove \(\max\{t_u,t_q\}=\Omega(\log n)\), together with update–query tradeoffs, in the cell-probe model with \(O(\log n)\)-bit cells. Here \(t_u\) and \(t_q\) measure update and query cost. The bound applies even to disjoint paths and permits amortization and randomization. Cell probes count memory accesses while allowing free computation, so a bound there also constrains a word RAM. A logarithmic lower bound is compatible with the requested polylogarithmic upper bound.

As checked on 15 September 2026, the official FOCS 2026 accepted-paper list includes Dynamic Connectivity, Minimum Spanning Tree, and 2-Edge Connectivity with Polylogarithmic Worst-Case Update Time, by Simon Meierhans, Maximilian Probst Gutenberg and Yu-Cheng Yeh. The inspected entry provides a title and authors, with no theorem or manuscript link. It does not specify whether the guarantee is deterministic. The current status is therefore recorded as uncertain; this announcement is neither treated as a verified matching solution nor ignored in favor of an older open-problem statement.

Probst Gutenberg’s publication page independently lists the same FOCS 2026 title and coauthors, again without a manuscript link in that entry. The conference is scheduled for November 2026; its acceptance announcement is distinct from an inspected proceedings paper. A complete statement is needed to decide whether the result meets this exact deterministic target.

sentences: The data structure receives edge insertions, deletions and connectivity queries one at a time on an initially empty undirected graph.
The question asks for one finite deterministic word-RAM program with exact answers, polynomial space and polylogarithmic time for every individual operation.
A complete Lean answer must establish all guarantees or rule out every program and every choice of the fixed constants.
Known amortized, randomized expected-time and deterministic subpolynomial results illustrate distinct guarantees around this target.
A newly announced FOCS 2026 paper may affect the current status, but the inspected title-only sources do not establish whether its theorem matches the deterministic target.
